title: SHE LIVED CLOSE TO HEROD’S PALACE—BUT HER HEART BELONGED TO JESUS.
paragraphs: SHE LIVED CLOSE TO HEROD’S PALACE—BUT HER HEART BELONGED TO JESUS.

Her husband managed the household of a ruler whose family was stained by violence and corruption. Yet Joanna used what she had to support the very Messiah that earthly power could never silence. Her story reveals something extraordinary about grace, money, courage, and what it truly means to follow Christ.
What happens when the woman connected to a powerful ruler’s household begins supporting a traveling preacher who announces a Kingdom greater than every earthly throne?
You might expect her to disappear from the story.
To protect her position.
To protect her reputation.
To protect everything she could lose.
But Luke records something astonishing.
Her name was Joanna.
And while history remembers Herod for his power, Scripture remembers Joanna for what she gave to Jesus.
Read that again.
One name was associated with a throne.
The other was associated with the Savior.
And nearly two thousand years later, the woman whose life could have been defined by proximity to political power is still teaching the Church what it means to belong to Christ.
Because sometimes the most remarkable evidence of grace is not where God found someone.
It is what they choose to do after encountering Him.
And before this story ends, you may discover that Joanna's testimony has something deeply personal to say about your own life, your resources, your fears, and the Kingdom you are actually living for.
Luke introduces her almost quietly.
No dramatic speech.
No elaborate biography.
Just a few words that carry extraordinary weight.
“And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance.” — Luke 8:3, KJV
There it is.
Joanna.
The wife of Chuza.
Herod's steward.
A woman whose name might have been forgotten if God had not chosen to preserve it in His Word.
But to understand the significance of that sentence, you must understand the world surrounding it.
The Herod mentioned here is generally understood to be Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee and Perea during Jesus' public ministry.
He was not Herod the Great, the ruler associated with the slaughter of the children in Bethlehem.
This was his son.
Herod Antipas was the ruler who imprisoned John the Baptist and eventually ordered his execution.

According to Mark 6:17–29, John had confronted Herod over his unlawful marriage to Herodias. What followed was a story of resentment, manipulation, a reckless oath, and a prophet's head delivered on a platter.
This was the political world surrounding Joanna's household.
And her husband, Chuza, held an important position within it.
Luke uses the Greek word ἐπίτροπος (epítropos) to describe Chuza.
The word can refer to a manager, administrator, guardian, or steward entrusted with another person's affairs.
In this context, it identifies Chuza as a steward associated with Herod's household or estate.
That tells us something important.
Joanna was not introduced as someone living entirely outside the structures of influence and authority.
Her family had a connection to the ruler's administration.
But Scripture does not tell us the precise extent of their wealth, the details of their marriage, or whether Chuza personally approved of Joanna's involvement with Jesus.
We should not invent those details.
The truth Scripture gives us is already powerful enough.
A woman connected to Herod's household became one of the women who materially supported Jesus' ministry.
Consider that for a moment.
Herod Antipas would later hear reports about Jesus and become perplexed about His identity (Luke 9:7–9).
Yet Luke had already introduced a woman connected to Herod's administration among those supporting Jesus.
The contrast is striking.
Earthly power was trying to understand the Messiah.
Meanwhile, Joanna was helping sustain the ministry through which His Kingdom was being proclaimed.
And here is where the story begins reaching beyond the first century.
Because you do not have to live near a palace to understand the tension of belonging to Jesus while surrounded by a world that does not honor Him.
Perhaps you work in an environment where integrity is inconvenient.
Perhaps your family does not understand your faith.
Perhaps the people around you measure success by money, influence, and appearances.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to preserve an image while privately wondering whether your life has become too comfortable to require real trust in God.
Joanna's story does not give us permission to speculate about her private struggles.
But it does give us a reason to ask about ours.
Who truly owns your allegiance when following Jesus begins to affect what you do with everything else?
Because the Gospel does not merely ask whether you admire Christ.
It calls you to follow Him.
And Luke's account becomes even more beautiful when we examine the women surrounding Joanna.
Luke 8:1–3 tells us that Jesus traveled through cities and villages proclaiming the good news of the Kingdom of God.
The Twelve were with Him.
And so were certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities.
Among them was Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.
Joanna was named alongside her.
Susanna was also named.
And Luke mentions many others.
Women whose lives had been touched by the ministry of Jesus.
Women who were not merely distant observers.
Women whose gratitude and devotion became visible in practical service.
The Greek text of Luke 8:3 describes their support with the expression:
διηκόνουν αὐτοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων αὐταῖς
diēkónoun autois ek tōn hyparchóntōn autais
The sense is that they were serving or providing for Jesus and His companions out of the resources belonging to them.
The verb διηκόνουν (diēkónoun) comes from diakoneō, meaning to serve or minister. Its imperfect tense portrays an ongoing or repeated activity.
This was not necessarily a single dramatic donation.
Luke depicts continuing practical support.
The women were helping provide for the needs of the traveling ministry.
And the phrase referring to their possessions matters.
They were serving from what they had.
Not from what they pretended to have.
Not from resources Scripture says they borrowed.
Not from wealth they were commanded to surrender under pressure.
From their own means.
Do you see the beauty?
The Gospel had reached their lives.
And now their resources were participating in the work of the Gospel.
Their giving did not purchase God's love.
Their generosity did not earn salvation.
Their material support did not make Jesus more worthy.
He was already worthy.
Their service was a response to the One who had brought God's Kingdom near.
And that distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because somewhere along the way, people began confusing financial giving with spiritual bargaining.
As though money could purchase divine favor.
As though God would only bless those who could afford to give.
As though the poor believer who offers a sincere prayer is less precious than the wealthy believer who funds an entire ministry.
That is not the Gospel.
Jesus never taught that salvation could be bought.
The apostle Peter condemned the attempt to purchase the gift of God with money in Acts 8:18–20.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Eternal life cannot be purchased.
Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But when grace truly takes hold of a human heart, it begins changing the way that heart sees everything.
Including money.
Including possessions.
Including influence.
Including opportunities.
Including the future.
The question changes from, “How much can I keep for myself?”
To something far more meaningful.
“Lord, how can what You have entrusted to me serve what matters to You?”
And suddenly Joanna's brief appearance in Scripture becomes deeply confronting.
Because she reminds us that following Jesus is not only about what we say with our mouths.
It is also about what we do with what has been placed in our hands.
There is another detail about Joanna that makes her story unforgettable.
She appears again.
Not in a palace.
Not beside Herod.
Not in a list of wealthy benefactors.
But in the account of the empty tomb.
Luke 24 tells us that women came to Jesus' tomb early in the morning, bringing spices they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away.
They did not find His body.
And two men in dazzling garments reminded them that Jesus had foretold His death and resurrection.
The women returned and reported these things to the apostles.
Then Luke names them.
Mary Magdalene.
Joanna.
Mary the mother of James.
And the other women with them.
Read Luke 24:9–10 carefully.
The same Joanna named among those who supported Jesus' ministry is named among the women who reported the news of the empty tomb.
Think about the movement of that testimony.
In Luke 8, she is associated with supporting the proclamation of God's Kingdom.
In Luke 24, she is associated with announcing the astonishing news that the crucified Jesus was no longer in the tomb.
From ministry support to resurrection witness.
From providing for the journey to bearing witness at one of the most significant moments in human history.
And although Luke does not tell us every event Joanna experienced between those chapters, the two references together reveal something remarkable.
Her connection to Jesus was not a passing footnote.
Her name appears at the beginning of His traveling ministry and again in the resurrection narrative.
The world may have known her through her husband's connection to Herod.
But the Gospel remembers her in connection with Christ.
And that should make every one of us stop.
Because so many people spend their lives trying to be remembered for things that cannot survive the grave.
A bigger house.
A more impressive title.
A prestigious association.
A growing bank account.
A reputation everyone admires.
But what will remain when those things are gone?
What if the greatest thing your life ever accomplished was something that never made you famous?
What if your quiet generosity helped someone hear the Gospel?
What if a book you helped distribute reached a person who had nearly given up?
What if a Scripture reflection you shared became the reason someone opened a Bible again?
What if the person you prayed for, encouraged, or helped never forgot the day you reminded them that Jesus still receives sinners?
You may never know the full impact in this lifetime.
But that does not make the obedience meaningless.
The Kingdom of God has always been advancing through acts of faithfulness that the world considers too small to celebrate.
And Joanna's name is proof that Scripture does not overlook those who serve.
Yet there is a danger here.
We can admire Joanna's giving so much that we miss the Savior at the center of her story.
Joanna is not the Redeemer.
Jesus is.
Joanna did not conquer death.
Jesus did.
Joanna's resources did not reconcile sinners to God.
The blood of Christ did.
And that is why this story must lead us somewhere deeper than an appeal for generosity.
It must lead us to the cross.
Because every human being, whether living near a palace or sleeping beneath a borrowed roof, stands in need of the same mercy.
Sin has touched every class of society.
It reaches the powerful and the powerless.
The wealthy and the poor.
The religious and the rebellious.
The person whose failures are publicly exposed.
And the person whose respectable appearance conceals a private life of compromise.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
No palace can protect us from that truth.
No religious title can erase it.
No charitable contribution can cancel it.
No amount of public admiration can make a guilty conscience clean before a holy God.
But then comes the glory of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our broken world.
He proclaimed the Kingdom.
He welcomed sinners.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He healed the afflicted.
He willingly went to the cross.
And there He bore the judgment our sins deserved.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The empty tomb Joanna and the other women encountered was not simply an inspiring ending to a tragic story.
It testified that death had not defeated the Savior.
Christ was risen.
And because He lives, repentance is not a journey toward hopeless condemnation.
It is a turning toward the living Savior who offers forgiveness and new life.
The person who has lied can repent.
The person who has betrayed someone can repent.
The person who has worshiped money can repent.
The person who has spent years hiding behind religious appearances can repent.
The person who has wandered far from God can turn back to Christ.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus is sufficient.
And maybe that is the part you needed to hear today.
You may have been reading about Joanna while quietly thinking about your own life.
The compromises.
The opportunities you wasted.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The Bible collecting dust.
The generosity you kept postponing.
The resentment you have been protecting.
The fear of what obedience might cost.
The version of yourself you present to others.
And the version only God sees.
You know what it feels like to appear stable while something inside you is exhausted.
You know how easy it is to say, “Lord, I love You,” while keeping certain rooms of your heart locked.
But Jesus is not calling you to manufacture a more impressive religious image.
He calls you to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
You do not have to clean yourself up to become worthy of approaching Christ.
You come because He is merciful.
And His mercy does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to turn away from sin and walk in new obedience.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved.
But power to begin living differently.
And perhaps one of the places where that change becomes visible is in what we do with the resources God has entrusted to us.
Joanna's example speaks directly to this.
But it must be understood correctly.
The New Testament does encourage believers to support Gospel ministry.
Paul explains in 1 Corinthians 9:14 that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel.
Galatians 6:6 encourages believers who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach.
Philippians 4:15–18 describes the Philippian believers' material partnership in Paul's ministry as a pleasing sacrifice to God.
These passages establish a legitimate biblical foundation for voluntary financial support of Gospel work.
But they do not authorize anyone to manipulate believers into giving.
They do not make supporting one particular ministry a test of whether someone truly glorifies God.
And they do not require a Christian to divert the resources needed for family responsibilities or local-church commitments.
Second Corinthians 9:7 gives us the governing principle:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
Not because someone frightened you with spiritual threats.
But willingly.
Thoughtfully.
Cheerfully.
As an expression of love.
That is the kind of generosity worth cultivating.
And it is the spirit in which I want to invite you into something deeply meaningful.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, find encouragement, or remember the beauty of Jesus Christ, you have an opportunity to help this work reach others.
Not because you owe us for God's grace.
You do not.
But because meaningful Gospel-centered work requires time, resources, consistency, and the willing partnership of people who believe that biblical truth should continue reaching hungry hearts.

For believers who choose to designate it that way, it may form part of their planned charitable giving. It should not be confused with a required biblical tithe, an automatic replacement for supporting one's local church, or a guarantee of divine blessing.
What matters is that your giving is prayerful, responsible, and freely offered to honor Christ.
And think about what that support can help make possible.
More Scripture-centered articles.
More thoughtful discipleship materials.
More biblical teaching.
More encouragement for struggling believers.
More resources for those seeking to know Jesus.
More opportunities to proclaim repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming grace of God.
That library exists to help believers go deeper in Scripture, grow in discernment, strengthen their faith, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
Because behind every resource is a potential reader.
And behind every reader is a real human life.
Someone fighting temptation.
Someone grieving.
Someone newly converted and searching for answers.
Someone ashamed of the past.
Someone wondering whether God could still forgive them.
Someone trying to rebuild a marriage.
Someone desperate to know whether the promises of Scripture can be trusted.
We cannot promise that every article will change a life.
We cannot claim that every resource will lead someone to salvation.
Only God knows the eternal fruit.
But we can faithfully make the truth available.
We can point people to Jesus.
We can keep opening the Scriptures.
And we can invite others to take part in that work.
These products are not the reason to follow Christ.
And no merchandise can replace a living relationship with Him.
They are simply another way to encourage faith, keep biblical reminders close, and support the ongoing work of this ministry.
But there is something else I want you to remember.
You do not need money to participate in spreading the Gospel.
Perhaps your household is going through a difficult season.
Perhaps every peso or dollar has already been carefully assigned to food, rent, medicine, or family responsibilities.
Please do not feel ashamed.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your standing before God.
You are not a lesser believer because you cannot contribute financially.
There are other meaningful ways to serve.
You can pray.
You can encourage.
You can tell someone about Jesus.
You can share Scripture.
And you can help this message travel beyond the people who would otherwise see it.
Someone among your friends may need this message more than you realize.
Someone who has become spiritually cold.
Someone who feels disqualified by their past.
Someone who has forgotten that the Gospel is not about earning mercy, but receiving it through Christ and learning to walk in His ways.
If a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them with kindness.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their private struggles.
But to let them know that the hope found in Jesus is worth sharing.
Not because the words themselves possess any special power.
But because the Scriptures behind them deserve to be revisited.
Return to Luke 8:1–3.
Read Luke 24:1–12.
Study 2 Corinthians 9.
Ask God to teach you the difference between religious pressure and Gospel-shaped generosity.
Not everyone who reads will agree.
Not everyone who encounters the Gospel will immediately respond.
But everyone deserves to hear the truth of what Christ has done.
What is the one area of your life you are still afraid to place completely in the hands of Jesus?
Is it your future?
Your reputation?
Your finances?
Your marriage?
Your secret sin?
Your fear of losing control?
Your inability to forgive?
Or the part of your past you still believe is too shameful for God to redeem?
You do not need to reveal anything publicly that would compromise your safety or someone else's privacy.
But perhaps this is the moment to stop pretending you have no struggle.
Your words may encourage someone who believes their own story is beyond redemption.
And if you are not ready to write anything publicly, take the question into prayer.
God hears you even when no one else knows what you are carrying.
Now return with me one final time to Joanna.
The woman whose husband managed affairs for Herod.
The woman who helped support Jesus and His companions.
The woman named again among those who reported the news of the empty tomb.
There is no biblical evidence that she gave away all her possessions.
No record that she abandoned her husband.
No account of a dramatic confrontation between Joanna and Herod.
No basis for claiming that she secretly financed the entire ministry of Jesus.
We do not need any of those invented details.
What Scripture actually records is enough.
She was connected to a powerful household.
She supported the ministry of Christ from her resources.
And she was named among the women who carried the news of the empty tomb to the apostles.
That is her testimony.
And the most extraordinary thing about it is not that she lived near power.
It is that her name became attached to the story of the One whose Kingdom will never end.
Herod's earthly authority did not last forever.
The political structures of his day passed away.
The wealth of that ancient world changed hands countless times.
But the risen Jesus Christ remains Lord.
And Joanna's brief biblical testimony still speaks.
Perhaps that is the question her story leaves with us.
Not whether we have enough influence to impress the world.
But whether we are willing to use whatever God has entrusted to us in faithful service to Christ.
For some, that may mean generous financial partnership.
For others, hospitality, teaching, prayer, encouragement, or quiet acts of mercy.
For all believers, it means recognizing that we belong to Jesus.
Our resources are not our savior.
Our reputation is not our savior.
Our generosity is not our savior.
Jesus Christ alone is our Savior.
And when His grace transforms us, even the ordinary things we hold can become instruments of love.
A meal.
A conversation.
An open Bible.
A voluntary gift.
A quiet prayer.
A testimony spoken through tears.
Do not underestimate what faithfulness can look like when it is offered to God.
And do not confuse the size of an offering with the depth of someone's love for Christ.
Remember the poor widow in Mark 12:41–44.
Jesus saw what others might have overlooked.
He saw beyond the amount.
He saw the heart and the sacrifice.
The Lord who noticed that widow also saw Joanna and the women who served.
And He sees the faithful obedience that no audience applauds today.
So when this article is over and the screen grows dark, I hope you remember more than Joanna's connection to Herod.
I hope you remember the Savior she followed.
The Christ who died for sinners.
The Christ who rose from the grave.
The Christ who still calls people to repentance and faith.
The Christ who can take a life marked by sin, regret, fear, and brokenness and make it a testimony of redeeming grace.
Perhaps your story has contained chapters you wish had never been written.
Perhaps you cannot undo what happened.
Perhaps there are consequences you must still face.
But your past does not have the authority to cancel the promise of forgiveness offered through Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Trust Him.
Turn from sin.
Receive His grace.
And follow Him with what you have, where you are, today.
Because the greatest miracle in Joanna's story is not that a woman connected to Herod's household helped support Jesus.
It is that the King of kings came into a broken world, welcomed people into His Kingdom, died for sinners, and rose again so that those who trust Him could have everlasting life.
Herod had a palace. Joanna followed the risen King. And only one of those kingdoms will last forever.
